articles.title: Councillor Calls for Urgent Meeting Over Disorder Reports in Middleton Town Centre
articles.excerpt: Councillor Lee Wolf has requested an urgent meeting with police and council officers following reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site, urging immediate action to address the situation.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

16:46, 28 September 2026

Councillor Lee Wolf has requested an urgent meeting with police and council officers following reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site, amid concerns from local residents.

16:34, 28 September 2026

Councillor Lee Wolf has urged for immediate action following reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site, calling for increased police presence and community safety measures.

Councillor Lee Wolf has called for an urgent meeting with Greater Manchester Police and council officers in response to increasing reports of disorder in Middleton town centre and at the former Durnford Street School site. In a post on a local Facebook group, he expressed concern that the area could become a 'no-go zone' for residents if immediate action is not taken.

Councillor Wolf highlighted that groups of young people have been entering the former school site daily, climbing onto its roof and throwing stones and mud at passing and parked vehicles. He noted that some parents have even dropped their children off at the site, which he described as inadequately secured. He is advocating for the installation of surveillance cameras at the location, including those capable of capturing vehicle registration plates.

In his post, Councillor Wolf urged residents to report every incident to the police to ensure there is an official record of the disturbances. Local residents have echoed his concerns, with reports of dangerous behaviour including a cyclist in a balaclava nearly colliding with a pedestrian and fireworks being directed towards shops and cars. Other incidents included fireworks being set off in bins outside businesses, and young people reportedly throwing fireworks and entering food shops near Tesco.

The councillor's call for action comes amid growing unease in the community regarding safety in the town centre. The meeting he has requested aims to address these issues directly with police and council officials, seeking a coordinated response to restore safety and security for residents.

articles.title: Four Arrested and £1 Million Worth of Drugs Seized in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police have arrested four individuals and seized drugs valued at approximately £1 million during a series of raids in Rochdale, following a six-month investigation into drug supply.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

16:45, 28 September 2026

Police have arrested four individuals and seized drugs worth an estimated £1 million following a major operation targeting a suspected drug supply network in Rochdale.

16:17, 28 September 2026

Police have arrested four individuals and seized drugs valued at approximately £1 million during a series of raids in Rochdale, following a six-month investigation into drug supply.

Police have arrested four individuals and seized an estimated £1 million worth of drugs as part of an investigation into the large-scale supply and distribution of illicit substances in Rochdale. Officers from the Serious Organised Crime Group (SOCG), supported by the Tactical Aid Unit (TAU), executed six warrants across the area on the morning of September 28.

The operation followed six months of meticulous detective work, which included surveillance and telecommunications data analysis. This intelligence gathering allowed officers to identify several premises believed to be involved in the storage and distribution of drugs on a significant commercial scale. One of the key locations raided was a property on Manchester Road, which appeared residential from the outside but contained vast quantities of suspected illicit drugs inside.

During the raids, officers uncovered a dedicated drugs storage facility and discovered a list detailing over 100 different types of drugs believed to have been supplied by the organised crime group. The haul included a significant amount of prescription-type medication, as well as bodybuilding and weight-loss drugs, spanning across Class A, B, and C categories.

The arrests and drug seizure mark a significant development in the ongoing efforts to combat drug-related crime in Rochdale. Authorities are expected to continue their investigations into the network involved.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Increases Parking Patrols Outside Schools to Enhance Safety
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has launched a new campaign and increased parking patrols outside schools to improve safety for children. The initiative follows reports of drivers failing to stop for school crossing patrols.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has launched a new campaign titled “Stop Means Stop” aimed at reminding drivers of their responsibility to stop for school crossing patrols. This initiative comes alongside an increase in parking enforcement patrols outside schools across the borough.

Councillor Dylan Williams, the council’s cabinet member for Highways and Facilities, introduced the campaign at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood. The council reported 137 instances over the past five years where drivers failed to stop for school crossing patrols, including cases where patrols had already stepped into the road. Cllr Williams emphasised the importance of stopping for crossing patrols to ensure the safety of schoolchildren.

The council is also urging drivers to keep yellow lines and school keep-clear markings free of parked vehicles. A crossing patrol worker at St Luke’s, identified as Chris, noted that vehicles parked on zigzag lines obstructed both his view and that of passing drivers, creating potential hazards for children crossing the road. A parent at the school suggested that families should consider parking further away to leave space clear near the crossing.

The increased parking patrols will be conducted without a fixed schedule, allowing for flexibility in enforcement. This initiative aims to enhance safety for children and ensure compliance with parking regulations outside schools.

articles.title: Matthew Moss Food Club Celebrates 10th Anniversary of The Bread and Butter Thing
articles.excerpt: The Matthew Moss food club, part of The Bread and Butter Thing, marked its 10th anniversary with a celebration attended by members and volunteers, highlighting its role in supporting the local community.
articles.content_html:
Members and volunteers at the Matthew Moss food club gathered recently to celebrate the 10th anniversary of The Bread and Butter Thing, a charity dedicated to alleviating food poverty. The event took place at the club, which is one of over 160 hubs across England that provide affordable food options to local communities.

During the celebration, attendees enjoyed cake and refreshments while reflecting on the impact of the food club. The Matthew Moss food club offers three bags of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, chilled items, and cupboard staples, for just £8.50. This initiative not only provides essential food supplies but also fosters community connections, allowing members to meet their neighbours and volunteer at the weekly hub.

The Bread and Butter Thing began its journey with a single van delivering surplus food to a community centre in Moss Side, Manchester. Today, it supports more than 100,000 households through its extensive network of hubs, demonstrating its significant role in addressing food insecurity across the region. Vic Harper, the charity's chief executive, emphasised the importance of community support, stating, "People knowing they can rely on us, week after week, is only possible because of the dedicated members, volunteers, and partners who make hubs like Matthew Moss such an important part of their community."

As The Bread and Butter Thing continues to grow, it remains committed to providing affordable food options and building community resilience. The Matthew Moss food club's anniversary celebration not only marks a decade of service but also highlights the ongoing need for such initiatives in the face of rising living costs.

articles.title: Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel: rock, history and the stories that grew around them
articles.excerpt: A riverside alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel is very real — the fairies that haunt it belong to a long local storytelling tradition rather than to the record of verifiable events.
articles.summary: A riverside alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel is very real — the fairies that haunt it belong to a long local storytelling tradition rather than to the record of verifiable events.
articles.body:
Stand for a moment by the narrow cleft of the Thrutch in Healey Dell and it is easy to see why people once spoke of a tiny chapel for otherworldly visitors. The River Spodden has cut a pulpit‑like niche and benches from the rock; the cleft, the surrounding mill remains and the dramatic Victorian viaduct are the things you can point to, map and photograph.

Those are the documented facts. Healey Dell is managed and described by Rochdale Borough Council as a nature reserve and visitor site with woodland, waterfalls, mill remains and a heritage centre. The Dell’s high railway viaduct — an important visible landmark — is recorded as a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England; the listing notes the viaduct dates from 1869–70 (listing first entered on 30 November 1984). The Healey Dell Heritage Centre and local walking guides explain the site’s industrial archaeology and contemporary visitor facilities. (Rochdale Borough Council; Historic England).

Where the fairies come in lies in printed and oral tradition rather than council minutes or building records. The best known early printed account of Healey’s supernatural associations appears in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published in the early nineteenth century), which collects versions of local romances and legends that include a “Fairies’ Chapel,” a miller, witches, a Fairy Queen and a small “Healey Dwarf.” Later nineteenth‑ and twentieth‑century local writers and the Dell’s own heritage materials repeat and retell those stories, sometimes in verse or in fanciful narrative form.

Local heritage interpretation explains the likely practical origin of the name. The “chapel” was a natural water‑eroded hollow at the base of the Thrutch that resembled an altar, pulpit and seats; Victorian tourists and local storytellers read human and sacred forms into these shapes and linked them to earlier folk beliefs. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre guide also records that a violent flood on 4 July 1838 reshaped parts of the Dell and destroyed some features previously associated with the chapel — underlining how the landscape itself, through erosion and flood, has altered the things people once saw there.

That combination of physical feature plus long local storytelling explains why modern references to a “Fairies’ Chapel” mix geology, industrial history and folklore. The accounts in Roby and in local guides are valuable as records of what people once believed and told; they are not contemporary evidence that supernatural beings exist. Claims that a Fairy King, witches’ covens, or a living Healey Dwarf actually inhabit the Dell are part of that folklore tradition and cannot be verified by archival records or official sources.

For residents and visitors the place works on two levels at once: as a real, protected landscape with listed industrial structures and as a pocket of cultural memory that has gathered tales for centuries. The Dell’s heritage displays, family trails and the local “Fairy Grotto” acknowledge that storytelling role while the council and Historic England listings record the concrete, documented elements of the site.

If you come to Healey Dell, bring both a torch for the paths and a readiness to listen. Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as a striking example of how landscape and local imagination meet — an important piece of our borough’s natural and cultural heritage, whether or not you believe in fairies.

(If you want to read the earliest printed versions of the Healey tales, consult John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire; for the site’s current description and visitor information see Rochdale Borough Council’s Healey Dell entry and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre materials.)

articles.title: Train Services Disrupted Between Leeds and Manchester Victoria Due to Cable Theft
articles.excerpt: Train services between Leeds and Manchester Victoria are facing major disruptions due to an attempted theft of signalling cables, affecting routes through Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

02:36, 28 September 2026

Train services between Leeds and Manchester Victoria are facing major disruptions due to an attempted theft of signalling cables, affecting routes through Rochdale.

Train services between Leeds and Manchester Victoria are experiencing significant disruptions following an attempted theft of signalling cables. This incident has resulted in cancellations and delays for trains running through Rochdale and surrounding stations.

The disruption is expected to last until the end of the day, impacting services at several stations including Manchester Victoria, Rochdale, Littleborough, and Hebden Bridge. Passengers are advised to check for updates before travelling.

In addition to this disruption, planned engineering work is taking place between Lockwood and Huddersfield, which will also affect services in the area. Trains will start from Lockwood or Penistone, with bus services provided between Huddersfield and these stations.

Passengers are encouraged to allow extra time for their journeys and to check the Northern Railway website for live updates and further information on service changes.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Launches 'Stop Means Stop' Campaign to Protect Children on School Runs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has initiated a campaign to improve safety for children during school runs, focusing on the importance of stopping for school crossing patrols and enforcing parking restrictions outside schools.
articles.content_html:
A new campaign aimed at improving safety for children during school runs has been launched by Rochdale Council. The initiative, named the 'Stop Means Stop' campaign, was introduced last week at St Luke’s Primary School in Heywood. The campaign seeks to remind drivers of their responsibility to stop for school crossing patrols, particularly as children return to school after the holidays.

Councillor Dylan Williams, the cabinet member for Highways and Facilities, emphasised the importance of this message, stating that there have been 137 incidents of drivers failing to stop for patrols outside schools over the past five years. This alarming statistic highlights the need for increased awareness and adherence to road safety measures during school hours.

In addition to the campaign, parking wardens will be deployed more frequently around schools to enforce parking restrictions. Councillor Williams noted that improper parking outside schools significantly reduces visibility, increasing the risk of accidents involving children. He urged drivers to be more considerate and to leave adequate space around schools during drop-off and pick-up times.

The 'Stop Means Stop' campaign is part of a broader effort to ensure the safety of children in the borough. As the school year progresses, residents can expect to see heightened enforcement of parking regulations and ongoing reminders about the importance of road safety around schools.

articles.excerpt: A Festival of Remembrance will take place at Rochdale Town Hall on October 16, recognising the service and sacrifice of armed forces personnel, with proceeds supporting local charities.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

Greater Manchester Police have initiated a murder investigation following the death of a 44-year-old woman discovered at a property on Tweedale Street in Rochdale on 25 May 2026.

14:55, 27 September 2026

A Festival of Remembrance will take place at Rochdale Town Hall on October 16, recognising the service and sacrifice of armed forces personnel, with proceeds supporting local charities.

A Festival of Remembrance will be held at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, October 16, to pay tribute to members of the armed forces community, both past and present. The event will feature performances by military bands, an act of remembrance, and the sharing of historic war stories, providing an opportunity for attendees to reflect and reminisce.

The Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, will be among the guests, alongside Members of Parliament, councillors, and dignitaries from across the Armed Forces. Councillor Rana expressed that the evening will be a special occasion for the Armed Forces community to unite in honouring the bravery and sacrifices made by service personnel.

Funds raised during the event will be directed towards the Mayor of Rochdale’s charities for the 2026/27 period. The beneficiaries include The Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club, Rochdale Women’s Welfare Association, SANDS (Stillbirth and Neonatal Death Society), Springhill Hospice, and The Christie.

This event not only serves as a remembrance but also aims to foster community spirit and support for local charities, making it a significant occasion for Rochdale residents.

articles.title: Vale of Lune Secures 32-28 Victory Against Rochdale in Season Opener
articles.excerpt: Vale of Lune triumphed over Rochdale with a 32-28 win in their opening match of the season, showcasing resilience and skill despite early setbacks.
articles.content_html:
Vale of Lune continued their winning streak with a hard-fought 32-28 victory against Rochdale in their opening match of the season. The match took place on Saturday, September 27, and marked the first meaningful encounter for Vale in the NW1 league.

The game began with an early setback for Vale as flanker Sam Walton left the field for treatment on an eye injury. Despite this, Rochdale quickly took control, scoring two tries to establish a strong lead. However, Vale responded with a determined effort, with Jordan Dorrington making a crucial break that allowed Ben McGarvey to score, narrowing the gap to 14-8 by half-time.

In the second half, Rochdale extended their lead with another try, but Vale's resilience shone through. With key players like Alex Briggs returning from injury, Vale rallied, scoring two tries in quick succession, including a debut try for prop Tadgh Butler. As the match progressed, Vale's confidence grew, culminating in a final try from McGarvey under the posts, which was converted by Jamie Mayall.

Vale of Lune's next fixture will be at home against Leek RUFC on Saturday at 3pm, where they will look to build on this positive start to the season.

articles.title: Who
articles.excerpt: The Healey Dwarf is a local figure of folklore tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel: a story preserved in 19th‑century collectors and retold by the modern heritage centre, not a documented historical person.
articles.summary: The Healey Dwarf is a local figure of folklore tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel: a story preserved in 19th‑century collectors and retold by the modern heritage centre, not a documented historical person.
articles.body:
Healey Dell — the narrow, wooded cleft of the River Spodden on the edge of Rochdale — has long been a place where geology, industry and imagination meet. Among the Dell’s best‑known tales is that of the Healey Dwarf: a small, ginger‑bearded figure who appears in nineteenth‑century collections as a companion or sentinel of the Fairy Queen and as the focus of stories set at the rock alcove locals call the Fairies’ Chapel.

The oldest printed witness I could find for the tale is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published 1829–31). Roby collected and shaped the stories people told around places such as Healey: his chapter on “The Fairies’ Chapel” records a local romance‑style narrative that links mills, a cavern‑like cleft called the Thrutch, a Fairy Queen and other folkloric motifs. Roby’s account is a literary record of oral tradition — valuable for showing what was being told in the early nineteenth century, but not a documentary or eyewitness record of supernatural events.

Victorian writers subsequently amplified the material. An 1882 book with the telling title Healey Dell, or the History [in Verse] of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel presents a fully dramatised, poetical version in which a character called Healey (often portrayed with a ginger beard in later retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and is imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later retellings helped fix the dwarf’s modern appearance: sometimes described as a tiny person who met the Fairy Queen, sometimes as a river‑borne “sentinel” or carved‑look rock that locals pointed to as the dwarf’s locus.

How does that square with what you can see today? The cleft called the Fairies’ Chapel is real: the Spodden has eroded a pulpit‑like alcove and bench‑like seats in the rock that easily invited romantic readings. Healey Dell is a documented nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology (corn, wool and cotton mill sites) and a striking Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed on the National Heritage List for England. Those facts are verifiable in council and Historic England records and are separate from the tales gathered by Roby and later writers.

The Healey Dell Heritage Centre and the site’s guide materials explicitly treat the Healey Dwarf and related episodes as folklore. The centre reproduces nineteenth‑century versions, stages family events around the Fairies’ Chapel theme and explains the geological and historical context that produced the chapel image in the first place. In short: the Dell’s guidebooks present the dwarf as cultural memory and storytelling rather than as a historical person or physically proven being.

If you want to trace the story yourself, start with Roby for the earliest printed atmosphere of the tale and then look at later Victorian‑era retellings that elaborated the dwarf’s appearance and adventures. When visiting Healey Dell, bring both a curiosity for the rocks, ruins and listed viaduct and an appetite for nineteenth‑century storytelling — both are part of what makes the place beloved.

A clear distinction helps: documented fact = the place‑name, the river‑formed alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel, the site’s industrial archaeology, the existence of a heritage centre and the viaduct’s listed status. Folklore = the Healey Dwarf as a supernatural individual, the fairy‑queen encounters, witches‑turned‑to‑stone motifs and prophetic episodes recorded by collectors; these are reported in printed folklore collections and local guides but are not independently verifiable historical events. Where specific claims cannot be found in archival or contemporary official records, they should be treated plainly as local tradition rather than factual history.

Whether you prefer geology, history or a good story, Healey Dell offers all three — and the Healey Dwarf remains a neat example of how a landscape can gather and keep stories across two centuries.

The centre reproduces nineteenth‑century versions, stages family events around the Fairies’ Chapel theme and explains the geological and historical context that produced the chapel image in the first place. In short: the Dell’s guidebooks present the dwarf as cultural memory and storytelling rather than as a historical person or physically proven being.

If you want to trace the story yourself, start with Roby for the earliest printed atmosphere of the tale and then look at later Victorian‑era retellings that elaborated the dwarf’s appearance and adventures. When visiting Healey Dell, bring both a curiosity for the rocks, ruins and listed viaduct and an appetite for nineteenth‑century storytelling — both are part of what makes the place beloved.

A clear distinction helps: documented fact = the place‑name, the river‑formed alcove called the Fairies’ Chapel, the site’s industrial archaeology, the existence of a heritage centre and the viaduct’s listed status. Folklore = the Healey Dwarf as a supernatural individual, the fairy‑queen encounters, witches‑turned‑to‑stone motifs and prophetic episodes recorded by collectors; these are reported in printed folklore collections and local guides but are not independently verifiable historical events. Where specific claims cannot be found in archival or contemporary official records, they should be treated plainly as local tradition rather than factual history.

Whether you prefer geology, history or a good story, Healey Dell offers all three — and the Healey Dwarf remains a neat example of how a landscape can gather and keep stories across two centuries.

articles.title: Middleton Writer Uses Horror Fiction to Aid Recovery from Alcohol Addiction
articles.excerpt: A Middleton woman, Alex Herod, credits her writing of horror fiction as a vital part of her recovery journey from alcohol addiction, exploring themes of trauma and mental health.
articles.content_html:
A Middleton woman who stopped drinking in 2019 has found solace and strength in writing horror fiction, which she says has been instrumental in her recovery from alcohol addiction. Alex Herod, who is currently pursuing a PhD in creative writing, uses her stories to delve into her experiences with addiction and trauma, allowing her to confront and process her past.

Herod, who has a diagnosis of complex PTSD, initially sought help through meetings, therapy, and sober communities before turning to fiction as a therapeutic outlet. She explained that while her stories are fictional, they often reflect her personal struggles with addiction, mental health, and transformation. "Writing horror has allowed me to go into very dark places and come out the other side," she said, highlighting how the genre provides a controlled environment to explore feelings of disgust and monstrousness that she associated with her drinking.

The act of writing has given Herod a sense of agency over her narrative, enabling her to express experiences she previously felt unable to discuss. She described this process as "making friends with my monsters," which has helped her learn to accept and embrace the darker aspects of herself, fostering a sense of connection rather than disconnection.

Herod recently shared her insights on the relationship between horror writing and recovery at a Recoverist Month event held at Manchester Metropolitan University on 15 September. She is set to release her debut novel next year, further integrating her journey of recovery with her passion for storytelling.
